title: Routine checkups
text: A routine checkup is a regular visit to a doctor when you are not unwell. It usually includes measuring blood pressure, heart rate, height and weight, asking about your lifestyle and family history, and discussing vaccinations or screening tests. Routine checkups help spot health changes early and give you a chance to ask questions.

title: Blood pressure basics
text: Blood pressure is the force of blood against artery walls. It is written as two numbers, systolic over diastolic, for example 120 over 80. Readings are taken at rest. A single high reading does not by itself mean a condition; clinicians look at repeated measurements over time.

title: What are vital signs
text: Vital signs are basic measurements of body function: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, body temperature and sometimes oxygen level. They are recorded at most visits so that changes over time can be compared.

title: Preparing for an appointment
text: To prepare for a doctor appointment, write down your questions and symptoms, list the medicines and supplements you take, bring relevant documents, and arrive a few minutes early. Being specific about when symptoms started and what makes them better or worse helps the visit.

title: Online consultations
text: An online consultation is a video or phone appointment with a doctor. It suits follow-ups, discussing results and some minor concerns. Find a quiet place with a stable connection. Some problems need an in-person examination, and the doctor will tell you when that is the case.

title: Understanding allergies
text: An allergy happens when the immune system reacts to a harmless substance such as pollen, dust mites, certain foods or medicines. Reactions range from mild itching or sneezing to severe reactions. Telling every clinician about your known allergies helps keep your care safe.

title: Medicine allergies and records
text: If you are allergic to a medicine, such as penicillin, it should be recorded in your health profile with the type of reaction and its severity. Keeping this list up to date helps clinicians avoid prescribing something that could harm you.

title: Diabetes overview
text: Diabetes is a long-term condition in which the body has trouble regulating blood sugar. Type 1 and type 2 are the main forms. Care often involves regular monitoring, balanced eating, physical activity and medicines chosen by a clinician. Regular follow-up visits are an important part of care.

title: Healthy eating
text: A balanced diet includes vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes and lean protein while limiting sugary drinks, heavily processed foods and excess salt. Eating regular meals and watching portion sizes supports steady energy and healthy weight.

title: Staying hydrated
text: Water supports temperature control, digestion and circulation. Needs vary with climate, activity and health. Pale yellow urine is a common everyday sign of good hydration. People with certain conditions should follow the fluid advice from their doctor.

title: Physical activity
text: Adults are generally encouraged to do at least 150 minutes of moderate activity each week, such as brisk walking, plus muscle-strengthening activities on two days. Starting slowly and increasing gradually lowers the chance of injury. Speak with a clinician before starting if you have a health condition.

title: Sleep health
text: Most adults need seven to nine hours of sleep. Regular sleep and wake times, a dark and quiet room, limiting caffeine late in the day and avoiding screens before bed can improve sleep. Ongoing sleep problems are worth discussing with a doctor.

title: Managing stress
text: Stress is a normal response to pressure, but long periods of stress can affect sleep, mood and the body. Helpful habits include regular exercise, breaks, talking with someone you trust, and relaxation techniques such as slow breathing. Support is available from counsellors and doctors.

title: Vaccinations
text: Vaccines train the immune system to recognise germs before you meet them. National schedules list recommended vaccines for babies, children and adults. Keeping a record of your vaccinations and asking your doctor which ones you may need is a useful habit.

title: Handwashing and infection prevention
text: Washing hands with soap and water for about twenty seconds reduces the spread of many infections. Wash before eating or preparing food, after using the toilet, and after coughing or sneezing. Covering coughs and staying home when sick also helps protect others.

title: Common cold and flu
text: Colds and influenza are viral infections of the nose and throat. Rest, fluids and over-the-counter symptom relief are commonly used for mild illness. Antibiotics do not work against viruses. Seek medical advice if symptoms are severe, last longer than expected, or you belong to a higher-risk group.

title: Fever in general
text: A fever is a body temperature above the normal range, often caused by infection. It is a sign that the body is responding to something rather than an illness in itself. Resting and drinking fluids help. Persistent or very high fever, or fever in infants, should be assessed by a clinician.

title: Cholesterol
text: Cholesterol is a fat-like substance carried in the blood. Having too much of certain types over many years can contribute to heart and blood vessel problems. Eating habits, activity, and sometimes medicines influence levels. A blood test measures them.

title: Body mass index
text: Body mass index, or BMI, compares weight with height. It is a simple screening tool and does not measure body fat directly, so it can be misleading for athletes, older adults and some ethnic groups. Clinicians consider it together with other measurements.

title: Reading lab results
text: Lab reports list each test with your result and a reference range. A value outside the range is not automatically a problem, because ranges vary between laboratories and people. Your clinician interprets results in the context of your symptoms and history.

title: Taking medicines safely
text: Take medicines exactly as directed on the label or by your clinician, keep them in their original containers, and do not share them. Tell your pharmacist about all other medicines and supplements you use. Missing doses or stopping early can reduce how well a treatment works, so ask your clinician if you are unsure.

title: Medication adherence tips
text: Pill organisers, phone reminders and linking doses to daily routines such as brushing teeth can help you remember medicines. If side effects bother you, talk to your clinician instead of stopping on your own.

title: Headaches in general
text: Headaches are common and often related to tension, dehydration, lack of sleep or eye strain. Keeping a diary of when they occur and possible triggers can help a clinician understand the pattern. A sudden severe headache or one with other worrying symptoms needs urgent medical attention.

title: Asthma overview
text: Asthma is a long-term condition in which the airways become inflamed and narrow, causing wheeze, cough and breathlessness. Triggers include allergens, exercise, smoke and infections. A personal action plan from a clinician explains daily care and what to do if symptoms worsen.

title: Hypertension overview
text: Hypertension means blood pressure that stays higher than recommended. It often has no symptoms, which is why measurement matters. Lifestyle steps such as less salt, regular activity and healthy weight support blood pressure control, and some people also need medicines.

title: Back pain
text: Back pain is very common and usually improves over a few weeks. Staying gently active, avoiding long periods in one position and good lifting technique can help. See a clinician if pain follows an injury, is severe, spreads down a leg, or comes with numbness or weakness.

title: Skin care basics
text: Daily sun protection, gentle cleansing and moisturising support healthy skin. Dry or itchy skin conditions such as eczema often need regular moisturiser. Any mole that changes in size, shape or colour should be checked by a clinician.

title: Mental wellbeing
text: Mental wellbeing includes how we think, feel and cope. Anxiety and low mood are common and treatable. Reaching out early to a doctor or counsellor, keeping routines, and staying connected with others all support recovery.

title: Pregnancy and antenatal care
text: Antenatal care is a series of check-ups during pregnancy that monitor the health of the parent and baby. Visits typically include blood pressure checks, blood tests and scans. Folic acid, balanced nutrition and avoiding smoking and alcohol are commonly discussed.

title: Child health checks
text: Regular child health checks track growth, development and vaccinations. Parents are encouraged to raise any concerns about feeding, sleep, behaviour or milestones. Keeping the child health record handy at each visit is helpful.

title: Your health records and privacy
text: Your health information is personal. Clinicians should only access the records they need to provide your care. You can ask which information is stored about you and who can see it. Use strong, unique passwords and avoid sharing your login.

title: Rescheduling and cancelling appointments
text: If you cannot attend an appointment, cancel or reschedule as early as you can so that the slot can be offered to someone else. Missing appointments without notice can delay your own care and that of other patients.

title: First aid for minor cuts and burns
text: For a minor cut, wash your hands, press gently with a clean cloth to stop bleeding, rinse with clean water and cover with a clean dressing. For a minor burn, cool it under cool running water for about twenty minutes and do not apply butter or ice. Seek help for deep, large or infected wounds.

title: Quitting smoking
text: Stopping smoking benefits nearly every part of the body and improves quickly. Support such as counselling, nicotine replacement and set quit dates increases the chance of success. A clinician can talk through the options that suit you.

title: Healthy ageing
text: Staying active, eating well, keeping social connections, attending screening and managing long-term conditions all support healthy ageing. Falls prevention, such as keeping floors clear and wearing supportive footwear, is also important.
